doc.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: How Dixieland changed: classic jazz, Chicago style and the revivalists
summary: Gordon dislikes the term Dixieland, tracing the music from 1920s black New Orleans artists through white Chicago players, the move to New York, and the 1960s revivalists like Marty Grosz.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: How has Dixieland — this could be a hard question, but we’ll try it — how has Dixieland music changed from, I don’t know, its New Orleans heritage?

Well it’s changed quite a bit. In the old days, I guess in New Orleans in the 1920s and even before that, they called it Dixieland jazz and they had mostly blacks playing that © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

type of music. And now, in the 90s now they have a whole different type of combinations of Dixieland bands. The name “Dixieland” is really a bad term because it puts a label on the type of music that actually was played. Actually it’s called “classic jazz” or “traditional jazz,” that’s what I like to call it. And back in the 20s when they had Johnny Dodds and Louis Armstrong and oh — Jimmy Noone, Mancy Carr, Lillie Delk Christian, Earl Hines, all these different stars in jazz in the 20s, were black artists. And they all sold millions of records. Louis Armstrong sold a million records in 1926 of his “Hot Five” and “Hot Seven” records. And through the years it has evolved, in Chicago, in New York, where more white musicians were getting into it now, getting into it then. I’m speaking of people like Bix Beiderbecke or Bud Freeman, Pee Wee Russell, Eddie Condon — there’s a whole slew of them which were called the Chicago style jazz. And these fellows were mostly white guys that heard Louis Armstrong and Johnny Dodds and all these people on riverboats as they traveled up the Mississippi River. And then from there, Eddie Condon, as I was saying before, Eddie Condon, Pee Wee Russell and Bud Freeman etcetera, they moved east to New York and in doing so, they brought in another flux of musicians, where the blacks started to come back in jazz very, very much so — like Fats Waller and James P. Johnson and oh, Art Tatum or anybody like that would come in. And then in the 60s, all these fellows that were playing that jazz in New Orleans and playing the jazz in Chicago were all dying off. And so in the middle 60s there were some people that decided to keep the jazz going. Now some of the people that are keeping it going are here today, I mean at this jazz festival. And one of the major outlets of the white, the older white jazz coming into the younger style of white jazz or black jazz or whatever you want to call it, is Marty Grosz, who is one of our contemporaries, and I’ve known him since when I was living in Chicago. And there was a few fellows like him — Marty Grosz, Frank Chace, Frank Orchard, Tut Soper, there was Little Brother Montgomery, there was Bob Skiver, there was a whole bunch of different guys that started — the revivalist guys that started bringing that Chicago style back and the New Orleans style back. And then just as they were moved into the 80s, they were getting a little bit older like myself, and Marty Grosz and guys like that, and then there was another influx of musicians who came around again on the younger side. Now the people that are playing jazz today in their 20s and 30s are keeping the flame so to speak, of keeping it alive throughout the 20s, you know, 20s through the 80s. And a lot of those guys are there today at this festival also.
